timeline.description: Hermann Golluber's Jonass & Co. brings the department store experience to Berlin's less affluent, with credit vouchers and layaway plans.
timeline.longDescription: Hermann Golluber, born in Gdansk in 1876, came from a family of merchants in Berlin's textiles and fashion industry. By the mid-1920s he was co-proprietor of Jonass & Co. AG and Baugesellschaft Zentrum GmbH, with a department store at Belle Alliance Strasse 7-10 selling luxury and second-hand goods and offering loans and layaway plans. Business expanded to a site at Lothringer Strasse 1, where Golluber commissioned architects Gustav Bauer and Siegfried Friedländer to build a second department store in the new functionalist style, with a restaurant and roof garden on the eighth floor. Opened in early December 1928 close to the poor Jewish quarter, it promised purchase vouchers and loans – an attractive prospect for the mostly impoverished local residents.

timeline.description: Boycott, dwindling profits and SA parades to Horst Wessel's grave force Golluber out; the Propaganda Ministry takes over the empty store.
timeline.longDescription: Jonass & Co. was one of the first Berlin department stores to be claimed by the Nazis. In 1930, Horst Wessel had been buried in the cemetery opposite the store, which became a popular location for Nazi rallies and parades; by 1933 the Nazis planned a propaganda exhibition in the formerly Jewish department store 'at the heart of the Reich capital, on Horst Wessel Platz'. In March 1933 the whole business was transferred to a high-rise building at Alexanderplatz 2 on a five-year lease. The boycott of Jewish businesses, steadily diminishing profits and the ubiquitous SA men placed Golluber – whose business partner had died in August 1932 – under extreme pressure. He left the empty Lothringer Strasse site to the Propaganda Ministry for its exhibition The East – Germany's Destiny, opened in December 1933 by Reich Minister Frick and Alfred Rosenberg. By then Golluber was no longer on the company board.

timeline.description: The company becomes a limited partnership under Johannes Horn and Else Vogdt – 'in preparation for the store's transferal to purely Aryan ownership'.
timeline.longDescription: In November 1935 the company became a limited partnership with long-standing colleagues Johannes Horn and Else Vogdt as personally liable shareholders. The Berliner Tageblatt commented on November 28, 1935: 'One can safely assume that the whole transaction is in preparation for the department store's transferal to purely Aryan ownership.' Initially Golluber retained a share worth 800,000 Reich marks. A year later Horn took over his position as managing director of Baugesellschaft Zentrum; in February 1937 the Reich treasurer demanded the register files of both companies, and one month later the company owning the Lothringer Strasse site was changed into a civil-law partnership – Golluber had no alternative but to admit Horn and Vogdt as shareholders with a 40 per cent stake. The site was rented for three years by the leaders of the Hitler Youth organization and converted to accommodate roughly 1,000 employees.

timeline.description: Golluber leaves the partnership and flees to the USA; the store later houses the SED's Central Committee and, today, Soho House Berlin.
timeline.longDescription: In May 1938, Hermann Golluber and his short-term business partner Hugo Halle left the partnership; the company was no longer classified as Jewish. After the November pogroms, Golluber and his wife Rosa were hidden for a time by Margarita von Kudriavtzeff of the American embassy, who probably saved their lives. In spring 1939 they emigrated to the USA; Hermann Golluber died in New York on August 18, 1939 – by the end of 1938 he had lost his business and almost his entire fortune. From 1938 Johannes Horn was sole proprietor; he leased the premises to the National Socialists and sold them in 1942 to the Hitler Youth leaders.

timeline.description: The store becomes the seat of the SED's Central Committee, is restored to Golluber's heirs in the 1990s, and is today Soho House Berlin.
timeline.longDescription:
After 1945, the former department store was owned by East Germany's ruling SED party and became the seat of the Zentral Komitee, party archive and Institute for Marxism-Leninism in the ZK of the SED. There was nothing to commemorate the Jewish owners or the building's time as headquarters of the Hitler Youth organization. In the mid-1990s, the property was restored to Golluber's heirs. In 2007 they sold the building to the exclusive British Soho House Club.

The site today

In fall 2009, the building which Hermann Golluber had built was reopened as an exclusive international club: Soho House Berlin, a meeting place for artists, filmmakers, media workers and business people. The former discount department store, which built up its clientele in the late 1920s with price reductions and layaway purchase plans, today houses Turkish baths, gyms and luxury apartments. The building is classified as a historical monument.
